passages.source_text: ὁ δὲ τὸν τοῦ πλούτου ἡγεμόνα καὶ φύλακα ὄφιν ἀνελὼν Ἡρακλῆς ὁ γνήσιος καὶ φιλόσοφός ἐστι νοῦς, ὃς πάσης κακίας γυμνὸς ὢν ἐκπερινοστεῖ τὸν κόσμον, ἐπιδημῶν ταῖς ψυχαῖς καὶ σωφρονίζων τοὺς ἐντυγχάνοντας, λέγω δὲ ἀνθρώπους ἐοικότας λέουσιν τολμηροῖς ἢ ἐλάφοις δειλοῖς ἢ κάπροις ἀγρίοις ἢ ὕδραις πολυτρόποις. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πάντα ὅσα ἀθλῆσαι λέγεται Ἡρακλῆς, νοερᾶς ἀρετῆς ἐστὶν αἰνίγματα. αὐτάρκως δὲ νῦν ἐχέτω τὰ εἰρημένα· εἰς γὰρ ἕκαστον εἰπεῖν οὐδὲ ὁ σύμπας χρόνος ἀρκέσει.

πλὴν θαυμάζω πῶς ταῦτα σαφῶς καὶ εὐσεβῶς καὶ ὠφελίμως ἀκαλύπτῳ τῇ εὐθείᾳ δηλοῦσθαι δυνάμενα οἱ πλαγίοις ἀποκρύψαντες αἰνίγμασιν καὶ μύθοις αὐτὰ προκαλύψαντες κακοῖς ὑπὸ σοῦ ἔμφρονες καὶ σοφοὶ εἶναι λέγονται, οἵτινες ὥσπερ ὑπὸ κακοῦ προαχθέντες δαίμονος σχεδὸν τοὺς πάντας ἐνήδρευσαν ἀνθρώπους. ἢ γὰρ οὐκ ἔστιν ταῦτα αἰνίγματα, ἀλλ’ ἀληθῆ τῶν θεῶν ἁμαρτήματα· καὶ ἐλέγχειν αὐτοὺς οὐκ ἔδει οὐδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν αὐτὰ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις εἰς μίμησιν προτιθέναι — ἢ αἰνιγματωδῶς ἐλέχθη τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν θεῶν ψευδῶς πεπραγμένα· καὶ ἥμαρτον, ὦ Ἀππίων, οἱ ὑπὸ σοῦ ὀνομαζόμενοι σοφοὶ ὅτι τὰ σεμνὰ ἀσέμνοις μύθοις καλύψαντες ἁμαρτεῖν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους προετρέψαντο καὶ ταῦτα ὑβρίσαντες οὓς καὶ θεοὺς εἶναι ἐνόμισαν.

διόπερ μὴ σοφούς, ἀλλὰ κακοὺς δαίμονας τοὺς τοιούτους νόμιζε, οἵτινες κακὰς ὑποθέσεις ἔργων καλῶν προεβάλλοντο, ἵνα οἱ θέλοντες μιμηταὶ γενέσθαι τῶν κρειττόνων τὰς τῶν λεγομένων θεῶν ζηλώσιν πράξεις, ἃς διαλεγόμενος τῇ πρὸ ταύτης ἡμέρᾳ οὐκ ἀπεκρυψάμην, λέγω δὲ πατροφονίας, τεκνοκτονίας, μίξεις ἀσεβεῖς μητέρων θυγατέρων ἀδελφῶν, μοιχείας τε ἀπρεπεῖς καὶ ἀρρενομιξίας καὶ μιαρὰς ἀρρητουργίας, πρὸς ἄλλαις μυρίαις τοιαύταις ἀθεμίτοις μίξεσιν. ὧν ἀσεβέστεροι οἱ ταῦτα ἀληθῆ δοκεῖν εἶναι θέλοντες, ἵνα τὰ ὅμοια ποιοῦντες μὴ αἰδῶνται. ὅπερ εἴγε εὐσεβεῖν ἐβούλοντο, ἐχρῆν αὐτούς (ὅπερ ἀρτίως εἶπον), εἰ καὶ ὄντως οἱ θεοὶ τὰ περὶ αὐτῶν ᾀδόμενα διεπράξαντο κακά, τιμῇ τῇ πρὸς θεοὺς εὐπρεπεστέροις τισὶ μύθοις τὰ μὴ σεμνὰ ἐπισκέπειν, καὶ μὴ τοὐναντίον (ὡς φατέ) καλῶν αὐτοῖς πράξεων γεγενημένων κακὰ καὶ ἄσεμνα περιβάλλειν σχήματα, ἅτινα ἀλληγορούμενα καὶ διὰ καμάτων μόγις νοηθῆναι δύναται καὶ ὅταν νοηθῇ τισίν, ἐκείνοις μὲν ἀντὶ τοῦ πολλοῦ μόχθου παρέσχον τὸ μὴ πλανηθῆναι, ἐξὸν μὴ μοχθῆσαι, τοὺς δὲ πλανηθέντας ἄρδην ἀπώλεσαν. πλὴν τοὺς εἰς τὸ σεμνότερον ἀλληγοροῦντας αὐτὰς ἀποδέχομαι, ὥσπερ τοὺς ἐκ τῆς Διὸς κεφαλῆς αἰνιξαμένους ἀναπηδῆσαι τὴν φρόνησιν. ἴσως δὲ ἐκεῖνό μοι πιθανώτερον ὅτι μοχθηρῶν ἀνδρῶν δόξαν θεῶν ἀπενεγκαμένων, ἐκεῖναι ἐτολμήθησαν αἱ ὕβρεις.

ἀπάντων δὲ τῶν θεῶν τὴν ποιητικὴν ἀλληγορίαν οὐκ ἀκόλουθον εὑρίσκομεν. αὐτίκα γοῦν ἐπὶ τῆς διακοσμήσεως τῶν ὅλων ποτὲ μὲν φύσιν λέγουσιν ποιηταί, ποτὲ δὲ νοῦν ἀρχηγὸν γενέσθαι τῆς ὅλης δημιουργίας. ἐκ φύσεως μὲν γὰρ τῶν στοιχείων τὴν πρώτην κίνησιν καὶ σύμμιξιν γεγονέναι, ὑπὸ δὲ τῆς τοῦ νοῦ προνοίας διακεκοσμῆσθαι. καὶ ἀποφηνάμενοι μὲν φύσει δεδημιουργῆσθαι τὸ πᾶν, μὴ δυνάμενοι δὲ ἀνεπιλήπτως τοῦτο ἀποδεικνύναι διὰ τὸ τῆς δημιουργίας ἔντεχνον, παρεμπλέκουσιν καὶ τοῦ νοῦ τὴν πρόνοιαν, ὡς συναρπάσαι καὶ τοὺς πάνυ σαφοὺς δυνάμενοι. ἡμεῖς δὲ φαμὲν πρὸς αὐτοὺς Εἰ μὲν ἐξ αὐτομάτου φύσεως ὁ κόσμος γέγονεν, πῶς ἔτι ἀναλογίαν καὶ τάξιν εἴληφεν; ἅπερ ὑπὸ μόνης ὑπερβαλλούσης φρονήσεως γενέσθαι δυνατὸν ἐστιν καὶ καταληφθῆναι ὑπὸ ἐπιστήμης τῆς μόνης ταῦτα ἀκριβοῦν δυναμένης. εἰ δὲ φρονήσει τὰ πάντα τὴν σύγχρασιν καὶ διακόσμησιν εἴληφεν (ὅπερ ἀνάγκη μὴ ἄλλως ἔχειν): πῶς ἔτι ἐκ τοῦ αὐτομάτου συμβῆναι ταῦτα γενέσθαι δυνατὸν ἦν;

οἱ τοίνυν τὰ θεῖα ἐπὶ τὸ αἴσχιον ἀλληγορῆσαι θελήσαντες (οἷον τὴν Μῆτιν καταποθῆναι ὑπὸ Διός) εἰς ἀπορίαν ἐντεπτώκασιν, οὐ συνιέντες ὅτι οἱ πλαγίως φυσιολογήσαντες ·περὶ θεῶν καὶ τὸ εἶναι θεοὺς αὐτοὺς ἀνηρῄκασιν, τὰ εἴδη αὐτῶν διὰ τῆς ἀλληγορίας εἰς τὰς τοῦ κόσμου οὐσίας διαλύσαντες. πιθανώτερον οὖν λέγειν ὅτι οἱ ὑπ’ αὐτῶν ᾀδόμενοι θεοὶ κακοί τινες γεγόνασιν μάγοι, οἵτινες ἄνθρωποι ὄντες μοχθηροί, μαγείᾳ μεταμορφούμενοι γάμους διέλυον, βίους διέφθειρον, τοῖς δὲ πάλαι οὐκ εἰδόσιν τί ποτ’ ἔστιν μαγεία δι’ ὧν ἔπραττον ἐδόκουν εἶναι θεοί· ὧν κατὰ πόλεις καὶ οἱ μόροι καὶ οἱ τάφοι φαίνονται.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.

passages.text: But the Heracles who killed the serpent, the ruler and guardian of wealth—the true Heracles—is also the philosophical mind. Naked of every vice, it ranges throughout the world, visiting souls and bringing those it meets to sound judgment; I mean people resembling bold lions, cowardly deer, wild boars, or many-sided hydras. Likewise, all the other things Heracles is said to have accomplished as labors are riddles of intellectual virtue. For now, let what has been said suffice, for not even all of time will be enough to speak about each one.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν τοῦ πλούτου ἡγεμόνα καὶ φύλακα ὄφιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the serpent, the ruler and guardian of wealth
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both roles attributed to the serpent and the genitive relation to wealth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἡρακλῆς ὁ γνήσιος καὶ φιλόσοφός ἐστι νοῦς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the true Heracles—is also the philosophical mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: Treats ὁ γνήσιος as identifying the true Heracles and φιλόσοφος as qualifying νοῦς; the καί is represented by “also.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: bringing those it meets to sound judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: σωφρονίζω can mean making someone prudent, self-controlled, or sound-minded; this wording suits the philosophical context.
πολύτροπος can mean manifold, versatile, devious, or many-natured; “many-sided” preserves its breadth without choosing only the moral sense “wily.”
νοερός concerns mind or intellect, matching the passage’s allegory of the philosophical mind.

source_issues.source_quote: Ἡρακλῆς ὁ γνήσιος καὶ φιλόσοφός ἐστι νοῦς
source_issues.issue: The placement of καί permits some variation in construing the predicates, including “the true Heracles is the philosophical mind” or “the true Heracles is also a philosophical mind.” The main rendering preserves καί and takes φιλόσοφος with νοῦς.

passages.text: Still, I wonder how those who concealed these things in oblique riddles and veiled them over with wicked myths are called intelligent and wise by you, when the things could have been disclosed clearly, reverently, and beneficially by the uncovered, straight way. As though driven on by an evil demon, they laid snares for almost all humanity. For either these are not riddles but true sins of the gods—in which case they ought not to have exposed the gods or, in the first place, set those sins before human beings for imitation—or the things falsely presented as having been done by the gods were told in riddling form. And the men you call wise sinned, Appion, because by covering solemn things with indecent myths they encouraged human beings to sin, and did this while insulting those whom they even believed to be gods.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s contrast between an unveiled direct route and oblique, concealing riddles.
ἐνεδρεύω evokes lying in ambush or entrapping, rather than merely misleading.
ἐλέγχω can mean expose, convict, or censure; “exposed” fits the argument that their sins should not have been publicized.
Under negation, τὴν ἀρχήν idiomatically means “at all” or “in the first place,” not merely “at the beginning.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν θεῶν ψευδῶς πεπραγμένα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the things falsely presented as having been done by the gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context contrasts actual divine sins with false mythic representations. A more formally literal alternative is “the things falsely done by the gods.”
σεμνός may mean solemn, venerable, august, or dignified; the contrast is with indecent myths.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν θεῶν ψευδῶς πεπραγμένα
source_issues.issue: ψευδῶς may be heard as modifying the alleged performance itself (“falsely done”) or the presentation of the deeds as divine. The surrounding contrast between true sins and riddling falsehood supports “falsely presented as having been done.”

passages.text: Therefore regard such people not as wise men but as evil demons, for they put forward wicked storylines for noble deeds, so that those wishing to become imitators of their betters might emulate the actions of the so-called gods. When speaking on the previous day I did not conceal those actions: I mean patricides, murders of children, impious unions with mothers, daughters, and sisters, unseemly adulteries, male-male intercourse, and defiled acts unfit to name, besides ten thousand other unlawful unions of this kind. Still more impious are those who want these things to be regarded as true, so that they may do the like without shame. In this matter, if they had really wished to act reverently, they ought—as I just said—even if the gods had in fact committed the evils sung about them, out of honor for the gods to have covered the indecent things with myths of a more seemly kind, and not the reverse: as you claim, when good deeds had been performed by them, to wrap them in evil and indecent forms. Such forms, when allegorized, can be understood only with labor and scarcely at that; and whenever some people understand them, they have given those people, in exchange for their great toil, only the benefit of not being led astray, though the toil could have been avoided, while they have utterly destroyed those who were led astray. Nevertheless, I approve those who allegorize them toward the more dignified sense, such as those who intimated in a riddle that practical wisdom sprang from the head of Zeus. But perhaps this is more plausible to me: once wicked men had won the reputation of gods, those outrages were dared.

lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόθεσις may denote a subject, underlying premise, or dramatic plot; “storylines” fits myths that clothe supposedly good deeds in wicked narratives.
The comparative can refer to those superior to the imitators, here especially the beings called gods.
The compound directly denotes sexual intercourse between males; the rendering avoids importing a broader modern identity category.
μιαρός marks pollution or defilement, while the rare ἀρρητουργία denotes the doing of things that are unspeakable or not to be named.

lexical_decisions.chosen: out of honor for the gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative phrase expresses the honor owed or directed toward the gods.
φρόνησις is prudent or practical understanding, while ἀναπηδάω supplies the vivid image of springing forth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: had won the reputation of gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποφέρομαι with δόξαν can mean carrying off, gaining, or winning a reputation.

source_issues.source_quote: ὧν ἀσεβέστεροι οἱ ταῦτα ἀληθῆ δοκεῖν εἶναι θέλοντες
source_issues.issue: The antecedent and force of comparative ὧν are not fully explicit. It may mean “more impious than these” or introduce a subgroup, “among whom the more impious are.” The main text uses the defensible contextual sense “still more impious” without forcing an antecedent.

source_issues.source_quote: τοὺς εἰς τὸ σεμνότερον ἀλληγοροῦντας αὐτὰς
source_issues.issue: The feminine pronoun αὐτάς may refer back to the actions or accounts implicit in the argument; its precise antecedent is not explicit. The English “them” preserves that referential openness.

passages.text: But we do not find the poetic allegory concerning all the gods consistent. To take an immediate example, in the ordering of the universe the poets say at one time that nature became the originator of the whole creation, and at another that mind did. For they say that the first motion and mingling of the elements arose from nature, but that this was ordered by the providence of mind. Although they declare that the universe was fashioned by nature, because they cannot demonstrate this beyond objection on account of the artistry of creation, they also interweave the providence of mind, thinking themselves able to sweep along even the most discerning. But we say to them: If the world came into being from spontaneous nature, how has it acquired proportion and order? These can be brought about only by surpassing intelligence and can be comprehended only by knowledge capable of determining them precisely. But if all things received their combination and ordering through intelligence—which necessarily cannot be otherwise—how could these things then possibly have happened to come into being spontaneously?

lexical_decisions.rationale: ποιητικός can mean poetic or belonging to poets; “the poets’ allegory” is a viable alternative, but the adjective is preserved directly.
The passage contrasts nature and mind as competing explanatory first principles; lowercase English avoids imposing personification beyond the context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on account of the artistry of creation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔντεχνος denotes what is artful, skillfully made, or governed by craft.
σαφής applied to people can describe those who are clear-minded, perspicacious, or discerning.
Here φρόνησις concerns the intelligence responsible for cosmic proportion and order, rather than specifically human practical wisdom.
The phrase can also be rendered “by chance” or “of itself”; “spontaneously” maintains the connection with ἐξ αὐτομάτου φύσεως earlier in the argument.

passages.text: Therefore, those who wished to allegorize divine matters in the more shameful direction—for example, that Metis was swallowed by Zeus—have fallen into perplexity. They do not understand that those who gave oblique accounts of nature concerning the gods have also abolished their very existence as gods, dissolving their forms by allegory into the substances of the world. It is more plausible, then, to say that the gods celebrated by them were certain evil magicians. Though wicked human beings, they assumed different forms by magic, broke up marriages, and ruined lives; yet to people of old, who did not know what magic even was, they seemed to be gods because of what they did. In city after city, both their deaths and their tombs are evident.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to allegorize ... in the more shameful direction
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative phrase describes the direction or resulting sense of the allegorical interpretation, not simply its method.
In the mythic example Μῆτις is the conventional name Metis, although the name itself also means counsel or cunning intelligence.
φυσιολογέω means discoursing or theorizing about nature, while πλαγίως marks the indirect or oblique manner.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ εἴδη αὐτῶν ... εἰς τὰς τοῦ κόσμου οὐσίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: their forms ... into the substances of the world
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the philosophical contrast between the gods’ forms or identities and the cosmic substances into which allegory resolves them.
μάγος here denotes practitioners of magic; the following μαγείᾳ confirms that sense.
The middle or passive participle can mean transforming themselves or being transformed; the context presents magical changes of appearance.
μόρος can mean death, doom, or allotted fate; its pairing with tombs favors “deaths,” though “fates” remains possible.

"translation_policy_text": "# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |

| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
